title: Balance declines with age, certified: postural sway rises with age (r=0.62 on foam) via a correlation test bit-for-bit vs scipy and base R

dataset.name: A public data set of human balance evaluations (BDS)
dataset.record: 50 subjects (ages 18-75), eyes-open foam and firm quiet standing (60 s, force-plate COP at 100 Hz)
dataset.citation: Santos DA, Duarte M. A public data set of human balance evaluations. PeerJ 2016;4:e2648. doi:10.7717/peerj.2648.

proposition: Balance declines with age -- a central fact of fall-risk. This case demonstrates and certifies that across a real cohort. For each of 50 subjects (ages 18-75), COP path length on foam and firm ground is computed by the certified swayMetrics; a newly-authored correlationTest relates it to age, reproducing BOTH scipy.stats.pearsonr AND base R cor.test BIT-FOR-BIT. Quiet-standing sway increases with age -- on the foam surface the Pearson correlation is r=0.62 (p=1.5e-6) -- and the age-sway correlation is stronger on foam (0.62) than firm (0.39): challenging proprioception with a compliant surface unmasks the age-related balance decline.

claims.statement: Pearson correlation of age vs foam-surface COP path length
Pearson correlation of age vs firm-surface COP path length (weaker)
the age-sway correlation is stronger on foam than firm

validation.reference: The new correlationTest op is validated against BOTH scipy.stats.pearsonr AND base R cor.test on the identical data -- a double reference. All three compute the Pearson correlation of age vs foam sway and its two-sided t-based p; the coefficients agree BIT-FOR-BIT (|diff| ~1e-16 vs each). The per-subject COP path lengths come from PhysioMoCap::swayMetrics (certified against the Prieto reference in the sibling case). The age-vs-firm correlation is reported for the foam-vs-firm contrast.
validation.data: REAL -- Santos & Duarte (2016) balance dataset (figshare), 50 subjects (ages 18-75), eyes-open foam and firm quiet-standing COP
validation.note: The reproducible findings are (1) correlationTest reproduces scipy and base R bit-for-bit; (2) sway rises with age, more so on foam. HONEST scope: (1) the correlationTest op is NEWLY AUTHORED (Pearson/Spearman CORRELATION with the two-sided t-based p, which the ecosystem lacked); (2) it reproduces BOTH scipy.stats.pearsonr AND base R cor.test BIT-FOR-BIT (|diff| ~1e-16 vs each) -- the identical closed-form Pearson r and t-based p, so the residual is the floating-point floor, NOT A CONVENTION AGREEMENT; (3) the per-subject COP path lengths that feed the correlation come from SWAYMETRICS, itself CERTIFIED bit-for-bit against the Prieto reference in the sibling sway-posturography-bds case, so the inputs are validated end to end; (4) the finding: quiet-standing COP path length INCREASES with AGE -- on the FOAM surface the correlation is r = 0.62 (p = 1.5e-6 on 48 df, ages 18-75) -- and the age-sway correlation is STRONGER on foam (0.62) than on firm ground (0.39), i.e. challenging PROPRIOCEPTION with a compliant surface UNMASKs the age-related balance decline, consistent with older adults' greater dependence on somatosensory postural control; (5) this is a cross-sectional ASSOCIATION, NOT CAUSATION, on 50 subjects with a single trial per subject/surface; run_simulation = FALSE (deterministic).

open_questions.q: This is a cross-sectional correlation with one trial per subject per surface; a longitudinal design would test within-person change, and the BDS's eyes-closed trials, repeated trials, and full Prieto metric set would let the age association be modelled jointly with vision and surface. The foam-surface path length shown here gives the clearest single age signal. Documented, not escalated.
